labels.ctaBody: An idea to explore, a prototype to improve or a component to industrialise? Tell us what you need so we can define the right engineering work.
labels.scopeNote: We agree the scope, tests and deliverables with you before work begins.
labels.projectStageTitle: At any stage of your project.
labels.projectStageBody: Whether you are an individual or a business, we can start from an idea, drawings, a prototype or an existing product, for a focused task or complete product development.

creativity-innovation.title: Product creativity and innovation
creativity-innovation.description: You have a problem to solve or an idea to develop. We explore possible solutions before you commit to a product architecture.
creativity-innovation.approach: We agree the comparison criteria with you: function, cost, available space, manufacturing and use. We then explore several mechanical principles and sketch them so that the options can be discussed and compared.
creativity-innovation.validation: Depending on the uncertainties, we can add initial calculations, a SWOT analysis or a focused proof of concept. These additions and the next steps are agreed with you.
deliverables: Technical concepts illustrated with hand sketches
A scoring matrix based on the agreed criteria
Recommendations and the next checks to carry out
creativity-innovation.outcome: Turn an open problem into technical options you can compare.
needs: Explore an idea without a defined technical solution
Rethink an existing product or mechanism

steps.title: Frame the problem
steps.body: Define the need, constraints and comparison criteria.

steps.title: Explore options
steps.body: Connect mechanical principles, materials and manufacturing.

steps.title: Choose the next step
steps.body: Score ideas against the agreed criteria and identify what needs checking.

faq.question: Do we need a specification first?
faq.answer: No. A description of the problem, intended use and known constraints is enough to start structuring your requirements.

faq.question: Can this stage include a proof of concept?
faq.answer: Yes, when an uncertainty warrants it. A proof of concept (POC) can be a simple test assembly or partial prototype that checks a principle with limited expenditure. The function to test and the success criteria are defined before it is built.

faq.question: How do you compare different concepts?
faq.answer: We agree the criteria and their importance with you: function, use, cost, space or manufacturing. The sketched ideas are assessed in a scoring matrix. Trade-offs and uncertainties remain visible when choosing which concepts to develop.

faq.question: Can you improve an existing product?
faq.answer: Yes. A problem with use, assembly or manufacturing can be the starting point. We examine the functions to preserve and the constraints to improve before proposing changes to the concept.

faq.question: Is an attractive idea already a feasible solution?
faq.answer: An idea still needs to be assessed against materials, loads, available space and manufacturing. Initial studies identify uncertainties and help decide what needs checking first.

faq.question: How does a POC differ from a complete prototype?
faq.answer: A proof of concept (POC) checks the feasibility of a specific principle or function through a deliberately limited build. A more complete prototype can examine several functions and their integration. A successful POC therefore does not validate the whole product or its readiness for production.

caseStudy.title: A mechanism that measures the water actually filtered.
caseStudy.body: The filter carafe needed to indicate when its cartridge should be replaced. DOMTEKNIKA developed the complete product and an economical mechanism for counting water volume. The project connects concept exploration, everyday use and integration into a physical product.

creativity-innovation.ctaTitle: Which idea would you like to develop?
creativity-innovation.ctaBody: Tell us how the product will be used and which problem it needs to solve. We can explore the most relevant concepts and define the first checks.

technicalFocus.title: From sketches to concepts worth testing.
technicalFocus.intro: At DOMTEKNIKA, concept exploration produces sketches and a comparison matrix. The criteria are agreed with you. Selected concepts can then undergo initial calculations or a focused proof of concept before more detailed development.

rows.title: Explore
rows.why: Several operating principles illustrated with sketches.
rows.check: Compare different solutions to the same need.

rows.title: Evaluate
rows.why: Scores against agreed criteria such as use, cost, space or manufacturing.
rows.check: Choose concepts to develop and make trade-offs explicit.

rows.title: Resolve uncertainty
rows.why: Where needed, a feasibility calculation or a proof of concept for a critical function.
rows.check: Check a decisive point before detailing the whole product.

mechanical-design.title: Mechanical design in Switzerland
mechanical-design.description: DOMTEKNIKA develops products and mechanisms for industrial companies and innovators, from the initial architecture to components prepared for industrialisation.
mechanical-design.approach: From the first prototypes, we relate material and assembly choices to manufacturing, use and the end of a part’s life. CAD helps develop an architecture that addresses these constraints and the product’s interfaces.
mechanical-design.validation: CAD models clarify interfaces and prepare validation. Depending on the project, development continues through prototypes, calculations or refinement for production.
deliverables: Documentation for the stage, including toleranced 2D drawings and a bill of materials where agreed
mechanical-design.outcome: Translate a required function into a feasible mechanical architecture.
needs: Design a custom part or mechanism
Improve a product that is difficult to manufacture
Prepare drawings for a prototype or production

steps.title: Define interfaces
steps.body: Identify loads, available space and interacting parts.

steps.title: Develop the solution
steps.body: Build the CAD design, material choices and assemblies.

steps.title: Prepare validation
steps.body: Define the checks and technical documentation.

faq.question: Do we need to have a design already?
faq.answer: No. We start where you are: a blank-sheet idea, sketches, CAD models, a prototype or an existing product. We then clarify the functions to develop, interfaces to preserve and constraints to address.

faq.question: Does design include manufacturing?
faq.answer: The documentation can support prototyping or production. Manufacturing, testing and industrial support are specified within the agreed scope.

faq.question: What can serve as the starting point?
faq.answer: Drawings, CAD models, sketches, photographs and observations from an existing component can help. We identify missing information for the requested work, particularly interfaces, loads and functional dimensions.

faq.question: How do you select a component’s material?
faq.answer: The choice depends on function, loads, environment, weight and the manufacturing process. Assembly and cost constraints are also compared to identify a material suited to the product.

faq.question: Why do tolerances matter?
faq.answer: They define acceptable dimensional variations in manufactured parts. In an assembly, these variations affect clearance, guidance and clamping. Tight tolerances should therefore meet a functional need.

faq.question: How is a component prepared for manufacturing?
faq.answer: The geometry and specifications are assessed against the intended process. Access, functional surfaces, tolerances and assembly steps are reviewed to prepare documentation consistent with manufacturing and inspection.

faq.question: How can maintenance and repair be considered during design?
faq.answer: Identify the parts that need inspection, cleaning or replacement, and the access required. Fasteners, disassembly and cable routing should account for these tasks and the operating conditions.

caseStudy.title: Lowering a screen while preserving the architectural view.
caseStudy.body: At the Velum Sky amphitheatre in Geneva, the guides had to remain hidden with the screen raised. During descent, the screen is fully cantilevered. DOMTEKNIKA designed the guidance, stiffness and lifting mechanism around these constraints, integrating a precise function into its surroundings.

mechanical-design.ctaTitle: Which mechanism would you like to develop?
mechanical-design.ctaBody: Describe your idea or the product you want to improve. If you have sketches, drawings or CAD models, they will help clarify the components, interfaces and manufacturing constraints.

technicalFocus.title: Designing for the whole life of a part.
technicalFocus.intro: From the first prototypes, we examine how a part will be manufactured, assembled, used and dismantled. These constraints inform geometry, materials and interfaces before the product definition is frozen.

rows.title: Production and assembly
rows.why: Intended processes, volumes, functional tolerances and assembly sequence.
rows.check: Adapt geometry, fasteners and drawings to the manufacturing methods.

rows.title: Use and maintenance
rows.why: Loads, wear, environment and access to replaceable parts.
rows.check: Size components and plan maintenance operations.

rows.title: End of life
rows.why: Disassembly, material separation and intended recycling routes.
rows.check: Assess joining methods and material combinations during design.

prototyping.title: Product prototyping and validation
prototyping.description: DOMTEKNIKA develops prototypes to test ideas in use, verify mechanisms and prepare the next stages of product development.
prototyping.approach: A prototype should answer a specific question: verify a movement, test ergonomics or demonstrate a function. We define what must be validated before choosing its construction and level of finish.
prototyping.validation: Testing informs design iterations. A functional demonstrator and a production-representative part serve different purposes; the scope is tailored to the decision you need to make.
deliverables: Prototype or demonstrator suited to the need
Design revisions for the next development stage
prototyping.outcome: Get practical answers before committing to the next development stage.

steps.title: Choose what to test
steps.body: Define the question and observation criteria.

steps.title: Build the useful prototype
steps.body: Match materials and finish to the planned test.

steps.title: Test and iterate
steps.body: Document observations and necessary design changes.

faq.question: Does a prototype need to look like the final product?
faq.answer: It depends on what needs validation. A POC can isolate a mechanism in a simple test assembly. Ergonomics requires a representative shape; robustness or service life requires suitable materials, assemblies and test conditions.

faq.question: Is a working prototype ready for production?
faq.answer: Not necessarily. Materials, tolerances, assembly and the production process may need a separate industrialisation stage.

faq.question: What can a prototype validate?
faq.answer: A principle, function, ergonomics, robustness or service life, depending on the build and the planned tests. We define the criteria before manufacturing. Conclusions remain limited to the functions, materials and conditions actually represented.

faq.question: Why build several versions?
faq.answer: Each test can reveal something to improve or an assumption to revisit. Successive versions make it possible to test changes and develop the design using concrete observations.

faq.question: Can you improve an existing prototype?
faq.answer: Yes. We examine its construction, results and the difficulties encountered. Changes are then focused on the functions or operating conditions that still need checking.

faq.question: How do you know whether a test is successful?
faq.answer: Before testing, define the function, operating conditions and expected result. Observations can then inform a decision: keep the solution, adapt it or carry out another test.

faq.question: How can we evaluate how people actually use the product?
faq.answer: The prototype and tests should represent the actions and conditions being assessed. Having relevant users handle the product can reveal difficulties with handling, understanding or assembly, which can then guide design changes.

caseStudy.title: Three- and four-wheel concepts brought to physical prototypes.
caseStudy.body: Aventor began in 2012 as an internal project. DOMTEKNIKA developed its electrical and mechanical architectures, studied three- and four-wheel configurations and built physical prototypes. The project shows the progression from a concept to a complete system, before a separate startup was established.

prototyping.ctaTitle: What should your next prototype demonstrate?
prototyping.ctaBody: Your sketches, models and existing test results will help us define what to test and choose a prototype suited to the decision you need to make.

technicalFocus.title: What should your prototype validate?
technicalFocus.intro: We first define what the test must establish: feasibility of a principle, function, ergonomics, robustness or service life. Success criteria then guide the materials, process and level of build. A prototype validates only the aspects it represents and that have actually been tested.

rows.title: Principle or function
rows.why: A proof of concept or partial prototype focused on the uncertain mechanism.
rows.check: Define the expected result; the rest of the product may be outside the test.

rows.title: Use and integration
rows.why: A functional or ergonomic prototype representing user actions and interfaces.
rows.check: Reproduce the conditions of use relevant to the evaluation.

rows.title: Robustness and service life
rows.why: A prototype with representative materials, assemblies and loading.
rows.check: Define loads and cycles; a mock-up alone cannot validate endurance.

simulation.title: Mechanical simulation and analysis
simulation.description: We size parts for assembly and operating loads. Our finite element calculations include nonlinear analysis with large deformations where needed.
simulation.approach: We define load cases from assembly and use: snap-fitting, supports, contacts and transmitted forces. The model accounts for geometry and material; nonlinear analysis is used when the behaviour under study requires it.
simulation.validation: Results are interpreted alongside their assumptions. They guide geometry changes and physical validation; injection studies are covered in our polymer expertise.
deliverables: Simulation results and analysis of critical areas
simulation.outcome: Support design decisions with calculations and clear assumptions.
needs: Study loads and deformation in a component

steps.title: Set the assumptions
steps.body: Define materials, loads and boundary conditions.

steps.title: Analyse behaviour
steps.body: Study loaded areas and compare variants.

steps.title: Guide decisions
steps.body: Connect results to design changes and physical tests.

faq.question: What do you need for an analysis?
faq.answer: Available geometry, proposed materials, loads and operating conditions. Missing assumptions are clarified before calculations begin.

faq.question: How does simulation complement physical testing?
faq.answer: It helps identify overly fragile designs before manufacturing and can reduce prototype iterations. It also supports comparison of variants and targeted testing. Even a favourable result must be checked against representative physical tests: its validity depends on the assumptions, material and modelled conditions.

faq.question: Do you perform nonlinear calculations?
faq.answer: Yes, including studies of large deformations. The model is selected according to part behaviour, material data and contacts. For a clip, for example, the study can examine assembly deformation and transmitted forces; results are then compared with relevant physical tests.

faq.question: Why do boundary conditions matter?
faq.answer: Supports, contacts and loads describe how a component interacts with its surroundings. An unsuitable representation can substantially change the results, even when the geometry appears accurate.

faq.question: How do you check whether the mesh is suitable?
faq.answer: We examine how results change with element size and distribution. The quantity relevant to the decision should stabilise; highly localised peaks also require a review of geometry and applied conditions.

faq.question: Can you compare different geometries or materials?
faq.answer: Yes. Variants can be studied under comparable conditions to understand their differences. This guides design while accounting for manufacturing constraints and the tests still needed.

faq.question: Can simulation estimate a component’s service life?
faq.answer: A fatigue study can estimate the effect of repeated loads when the operating cycles and material data are appropriate for the case. A static calculation alone cannot establish service life; assumptions and the need for physical tests must be considered.

caseStudy.title: From calculations to a PEEK component prepared for production.
caseStudy.body: The acetabular reamer holder’s PEEK components had to meet both mechanical and injection moulding constraints. Finite element calculations and rheological analyses guided geometry optimisation. The work continued through tooling and refinement of the production process.

simulation.ctaTitle: Which technical decision do you need to verify?
simulation.ctaBody: Share your geometry, proposed materials and load cases. We can define the analysis scope and the results needed to inform your decision.

technicalFocus.title: Sizing parts for assembly and use.
technicalFocus.intro: We calculate stress and deformation to guide part sizing. Studies cover assembly loads, such as snap-fitting, and loads encountered in service. Large deformations can be addressed through nonlinear analysis, using assumptions suited to the material and contacts.

rows.title: Assembly
rows.why: Forces and deformation during snap-fitting or installation.
rows.check: Adjust geometry to enable assembly and limit loading.

rows.title: Use
rows.why: Stress, displacement and sensitive areas under the intended loads.
rows.check: Compare materials and sections to preserve the required function.

rows.title: Large deformations
rows.why: Changes in behaviour when deformation affects the response of the part.
rows.check: Select a suitable nonlinear model and plan comparison with physical tests.

polymer-injection.title: Polymers and injection moulding
polymer-injection.description: You are developing a moulded component or considering a material change. We connect design, mechanical behaviour and manufacturing constraints from the start.
polymer-injection.approach: Wall thickness, assemblies, material properties and operating conditions are studied together. Depending on the project, mechanical calculations and rheological analyses help refine geometry before tooling.
polymer-injection.validation: Our work ranges from component design to tooling coordination and initial moulded production runs. Trials check real behaviour and inform process adjustments.
deliverables: Geometry recommendations and analysis as needed
Tooling documentation and trial support within the agreed scope
polymer-injection.outcome: Develop the part and its injection moulding process together.
needs: Adapt a part for injection moulding
Replace a metal architecture with a polymer

steps.title: Choose the architecture
steps.body: Relate material properties to the intended use.

steps.title: Prepare moulding
steps.body: Study geometry, filling and critical areas.

steps.title: Refine production
steps.body: Support tooling, trials and initial parts as required.

faq.question: When should we involve you?
faq.answer: Ideally before fixing the geometry or commissioning tooling. We can also analyse difficulties with an existing component.

faq.question: Can you support initial production runs?
faq.answer: We have coordinated tooling, injection trials and initial production runs. DOMTEKNIKA’s role and the partners’ roles are agreed for each project.

faq.question: Why consider injection moulding during design?
faq.answer: Geometry affects filling, cooling and ejection. Considering wall thickness, draft and tooling access during design helps limit changes later in development.

faq.question: Can a prototype component be injection moulded unchanged?
faq.answer: Not always. A geometry developed for a prototype may need changes to its walls, ejection or assembly. The production material and process must be considered before specifying tooling.

faq.question: How do you select a polymer?
faq.answer: The choice depends on use, loads, temperatures, environment and the processing method. Material properties are assessed together with component geometry and product requirements.

faq.question: What is checked on the first moulded components?
faq.answer: Dimensions, appearance, assembly and function are assessed against the intended requirements. Observations identify any changes to geometry, tooling or process needed before production continues.

faq.question: Is injection moulding suitable for small production runs?
faq.answer: It can be, but tooling cost, quantities, geometry and material must be compared. The choice depends on total cost and product requirements, before investing in a mould.

caseStudy.title: Rethinking a surgical instrument in polymer.
caseStudy.body: The ZipFix implant applicator replaces a reusable steel architecture with an ergonomic single-use polymer solution. DOMTEKNIKA designed the product, built functional prototypes and coordinated an initial moulded production run. Material, use and manufacturing were considered together.

polymer-injection.ctaTitle: Is your component ready for injection moulding?
polymer-injection.ctaBody: Share your drawings, proposed material and production volumes. We can review part geometry, the process and tooling constraints.

technicalFocus.title: A strong part starts with considered wall geometry.
technicalFocus.intro: In injection moulding, geometry influences filling, cooling and ejection. Changes in thickness can cause local shrinkage and distortion. Addressing these constraints during design makes discussions with the toolmaker and initial adjustments easier.

rows.title: Walls and ribs
rows.why: A bulky section cools differently; a rib can add stiffness with less material.
rows.check: Consistent thickness and the junctions between ribs and walls.

rows.title: Draft and radii
rows.why: Draft helps ejection; radii soften transitions in shape.
rows.check: Ejection direction, surface texture and loaded areas.

rows.title: Mould separation
rows.why: Undercuts and access requirements may require additional tool movements.
rows.check: The parting line, acceptable marks and functional surfaces.

electronics-integration.title: Electrical and electronics integration
electronics-integration.description: DOMTEKNIKA integrates electrical and electronic functions into the mechanical architecture of products and demonstrators.
electronics-integration.approach: Development begins with the required functions and interfaces: power supply, control, components and packaging. Integration is considered alongside the mechanics to create a coherent, accessible system.
electronics-integration.validation: Our projects include electric mobility architectures and an automatically synchronised clock. Development depth, testing and preparation for production are defined around each project.
deliverables: Prototype and functional checks within the agreed scope
electronics-integration.outcome: Make mechanics, power supply and control work together.
needs: Add an electrical function to a product
Resolve interfaces between components and mechanics

steps.title: Integrate components
steps.body: Plan packaging, assembly and access within the product.

faq.question: Can you work with our electronics team?
faq.answer: Yes. We can focus on interfaces and mechanical integration, coordinating with your project teams or partners.

faq.question: What information should we prepare?
faq.answer: Required functions, selected components, power constraints and available drawings. We then define the necessary development work and checks.

faq.question: What does electronics integration cover?
faq.answer: It covers component placement, power, connections and interfaces with the mechanical design. Any electronics design or software work needed is defined in the project scope.

faq.question: Do the components need to be selected already?
faq.answer: No. Work can start from required functions or components you already have. Data sheets, dimensions and power requirements then help define the architecture and integration constraints.

faq.question: Why does the enclosure affect electronics?
faq.answer: It determines available space, mounting, cable routing and access to connections. It also contributes to heat removal; these constraints are addressed together with the product’s operating conditions.

faq.question: How is the combined mechanical and electronic system tested?
faq.answer: Interfaces are checked progressively: power, control, movement and behaviour during use. Tests should match the required functions and intended operating conditions, with criteria defined in advance.

faq.question: How can the runtime of a battery-powered product be estimated?
faq.answer: Account for consumption in each operating mode, the time spent in those modes and the usable battery capacity. Standby consumption matters too. An estimate based on the intended use should then be checked against measurements on the system.

caseStudy.title: Telling the time without a visible central pivot.
caseStudy.body: The transparent clock combines peripherally driven discs with automatic atomic-clock synchronisation. DOMTEKNIKA developed the complete electrical and mechanical concept, coordinated the design study and built a working prototype with moulded gear segments. Integration makes the product’s visual principle possible.

electronics-integration.ctaTitle: Which functions would you like to integrate?
electronics-integration.ctaBody: Tell us about the required functions, components and power or enclosure constraints. We can define the interfaces and the checks needed.

technicalFocus.title: Electronics integration also depends on mechanics.
technicalFocus.intro: Integrating a board, sensor or motor requires space for connections, mounting and operating conditions. The mechanical enclosure also influences access, wiring and heat removal. These interfaces need defining as part of the product architecture.

rows.title: Power supply
rows.why: Current at start-up or during an action can differ from average consumption.
rows.check: Operating modes, current peaks and connections.

rows.title: Space and access
rows.why: A connector needs room to be plugged in; replaceable components need access.
rows.check: Reserved volumes, cable routing and assembly sequence.

rows.title: Heat
rows.why: Power losses heat components; the board and enclosure contribute to the thermal path.
rows.check: The environment, heat to remove and its path to the outside.
